lines.t: Hello, everyone. In earlier lectures we spent a lot of time on mitigation, which means reducing the emissions that cause climate change.
Today we turn to adaptation, which means preparing cities for the changes that are already under way.
The distinction matters, because the two require different decisions and often compete for the same budget.
Cities are particularly exposed for three reasons. First, they concentrate people and property, so one flood can affect hundreds of thousands of residents.
Second, they are built of materials such as concrete and asphalt that absorb heat, which creates the urban heat island effect.
On a summer night a dense city centre can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside.
Third, many cities sit on rivers or coasts, because that is where trade began centuries ago.
Let us look at heat first. The most effective measures are surprisingly modest.
Planting trees along streets reduces surface temperature, and paler roofs reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it.
Some cities have opened cooling centres, public buildings with air conditioning, for people who cannot cool their homes.
The older population, and those living alone, are the most at risk.
The success of such a scheme depends on whether officials know who these people are and can reach them. A cooling centre nobody visits protects nobody.
Flooding is a different challenge. The traditional solution was to build bigger pipes and higher walls, an approach called grey infrastructure.
It works up to a point, but each wall has a limit, and when it is exceeded the damage can be severe.
Many planners now favour the sponge city idea. Instead of moving water away as fast as possible, the city is designed to hold it.
That means parks that can safely flood, pavements that let rain soak through, and roofs covered with plants.
These green solutions are often cheaper to maintain and offer other benefits, such as shade and wildlife.
However, they need space, and space in a crowded centre is expensive.
This leads to the hardest question, which is who pays and who benefits.
Studies from several cities show that wealthy districts tend to receive protection first, partly because they have more political influence and better data about their own needs.
Poorer districts often have worse drainage and fewer trees. So adaptation can widen inequality unless funding rules are explicit.
One approach is to rank projects by the number of vulnerable people protected per pound spent, rather than by the value of the property saved.
There is also the question of timing. Infrastructure lasts fifty years or more, so a decision made today must work in a climate we can only estimate.
Engineers therefore speak of flexible design: building a wall that can be raised later, instead of building the highest wall at once.
It costs slightly more at the start, but it avoids paying for protection that may never be needed.
To conclude, successful adaptation combines physical measures with social planning.
Cities that do best identify their most vulnerable residents, mix green and grey solutions, and review their plans regularly.
Your task this week is to choose a city you know and find out one measure it has taken against either heat or flooding.

qs.q: How does the lecturer define adaptation?
o: Cutting the emissions that cause climate change.
Preparing cities for changes already happening.
Moving residents away from coastal areas.
qs.why: التكيف يعني تهيئة المدن للتغيرات الجارية، أما التخفيف فخفض الانبعاثات.

qs.q: Dense city centres create the urban heat ___ effect.
qs.why: ذكر تأثير الجزيرة الحرارية الحضرية بسبب الإسمنت والإسفلت.

qs.q: What does the success of a cooling centre depend on?
o: Reaching the people who are most at risk.
Having the newest air conditioning.
Opening only on summer nights.
qs.why: ينجح المركز إن عرف المسؤولون الفئات المعرضة للخطر ووصلوا إليها.

qs.q: What is the limitation of grey infrastructure?
o: It cannot be built near rivers.
It is always cheaper than green solutions.
Damage can be severe once a wall's limit is exceeded.
qs.why: لكل جدار حدّ، وإذا تجاوزه الماء قد يكون الضرر كبيرا.

qs.q: The lecturer says green flood solutions are usually more expensive to maintain than grey ones.
qs.why: قال إنها غالبا أرخص صيانة وتقدم فوائد أخرى كالظل، لكنها تحتاج مساحة.

qs.q: Why do wealthy districts often receive protection first?
o: They pay higher taxes only.
They have more influence and better data.
They are always closer to rivers.
qs.why: لهم نفوذ سياسي أكبر وبيانات أفضل عن احتياجاتهم.

qs.q: How could funding rules make adaptation fairer?
o: By ranking projects by vulnerable people protected per pound.
By choosing projects according to property value.
By giving each district equal money.
qs.why: اقترح ترتيب المشاريع بعدد الضعفاء المحميين لكل جنيه لا بقيمة العقارات.

qs.q: What is the advantage of flexible design?
o: The highest wall is built first.
Protection can be increased later if needed.
Maintenance is no longer necessary.
qs.why: يمكن رفع الجدار لاحقا فلا يُدفع ثمن حماية قد لا تلزم.

lines.t: Good morning. Every legal system must answer one question: how can a court discover what really happened?
Today we trace how the answer has changed, from oaths to forensic science.
In many early societies, a court relied less on what had happened than on who was speaking.
An accused person might swear an oath, and bring neighbours to swear that his oath was trustworthy.
These oath helpers had not seen the event; they vouched for his character. The logic was social: a person with many respectable supporters was assumed to be honest.
Over time, this approach was replaced by testimony. By the later middle ages, courts in many places had begun to question witnesses directly.
The idea of two eyewitnesses as a standard of proof appeared in several legal traditions. It seems a sensible rule, yet it had a weakness.
It made it almost impossible to convict anyone when a crime occurred in private, and it gave great power to anyone willing to lie, since two false witnesses were enough.
The next major change was the rise of documents. As trade expanded, written contracts, receipts and records became the best proof of what people had agreed.
Courts began to ask for the original paper and to check seals and signatures.
This created a new problem, forgery, and so the first experts in handwriting appeared in courtrooms.
In the nineteenth century, science entered the courtroom. Early forensic methods included the comparison of fingerprints and chemical tests for poison.
Fingerprints were attractive because no two people were thought to have the same pattern.
A print left at a scene was physical evidence that could not be bribed or frightened. Courts quickly came to value such material.
Indeed, some lawyers began to complain that jurors were too impressed by anything described as scientific.
That concern proved to be justified.
In the twentieth century, a number of forensic techniques, such as hair comparison and bite mark analysis, were accepted for decades before anyone tested how reliable they were.
When researchers finally measured error rates, several methods performed much worse than expected. Reviews by scientific bodies called for stricter validation.
Today many courts apply tests before admitting an expert opinion: has the method been tested, has it been reviewed by other scientists, and is its error rate known?
The most recent revolution is genetic profiling, which began in the nineteen eighties.
It was the first method that could both identify a guilty person with extraordinary precision and prove the innocence of someone already in prison.
Hundreds of wrongful convictions around the world have been corrected as a result. But genetic evidence has also taught a lesson: even excellent evidence can be misunderstood.
A match statistic, explained badly, can mislead a jury as much as a weak fingerprint.
So the history of evidence is not simply a story of progress from superstition to science.
It is a story of changing trust: first in reputation, then in witnesses, then in documents, and now in laboratories. Each stage solved one problem and created another.
For next week, read the short article on the reading list about admissibility, and prepare two questions.

qs.q: What was the role of oath helpers in early courts?
o: They had watched the event.
They spoke for the character of the accused.
They examined documents.
qs.why: لم يشهدوا الواقعة بل زكّوا شخصية المتهم أمام المحكمة.

qs.q: What was a weakness of the rule requiring two eyewitnesses?
o: It could not be applied to written contracts.
It was too expensive for courts.
Private crimes were nearly impossible to prove.
qs.why: من الصعب إدانة أحد في جريمة وقعت سرا، ويكفي شاهدا زور.

qs.q: Why did handwriting experts appear in courtrooms?
o: To deal with forged documents.
To teach judges to read.
To replace the use of seals.
qs.why: ازدياد الوثائق خلق مشكلة التزوير فظهر خبراء الخط.

qs.q: Fingerprints were valued as physical evidence that could not be ___ or frightened.
qs.why: ذكر أن البصمة دليل مادي لا يمكن رشوته أو تخويفه.

qs.q: Hair comparison was tested for reliability before courts began to accept it.
qs.why: قُبلت هذه التقنيات عقودا قبل أن يختبر أحد مدى موثوقيتها.

qs.q: One question courts now ask is whether the method's ___ rate is known.
qs.why: من أسئلة القبول: هل اختُبرت الطريقة وهل روجعت وهل معدل خطئها معروف.

qs.q: What made genetic profiling special?
o: It was cheaper than fingerprints.
It could both identify offenders and clear prisoners.
It needed no expert to explain it.
qs.why: حدد المذنب بدقة وأثبت براءة سجناء، فصُحّحت مئات الإدانات الخاطئة.

qs.q: What is the lecturer's overall view of the history of evidence?
o: A simple story of progress to science.
A story of decline in honesty.
A story of changing trust, each stage creating new problems.
qs.why: قال إنها ليست تقدما بسيطا بل تغيّر في موضع الثقة، وكل مرحلة حلّت مشكلة وخلقت أخرى.

lines.t: Good afternoon. Language models now draft emails, summarise reports and answer questions, and people often describe them as if they understood language the way we do.
This lecture explains, in simple terms, what these systems actually do when they produce a sentence.
Let me start with the basic task. A language model is trained to predict the next piece of text.
Given the words, the cat sat on the, it estimates which word is most likely to come next. Mat is likely; refrigerator is much less so.
That is the entire training goal. Everything else, including the ability to answer questions, emerges from doing this prediction extremely well over enormous quantities of text.
The unit is not exactly a word. The text is first cut into tokens, which are short pieces, sometimes whole words, sometimes parts of a word.
A rare name might be split into three or four tokens, while a common word is usually a single one.
This explains why models sometimes make odd mistakes with spelling or counting letters: they never see the letters directly.
Next, how does the model decide? Inside it is a very large network of numbers, called parameters, which were adjusted during training.
Modern systems use a design called the transformer, whose key component is attention.
Attention allows the model, at each step, to look back at the earlier tokens and decide which ones matter most for the next prediction.
In the sentence, the lawyer told the client that she would win, attention helps the model work out who she refers to, based on patterns seen in training.
The output of the network is not one word but a probability for every possible token. Then comes a choice.
If the system always chose the most probable token, its text would be dull and repetitive. So a setting called temperature controls the randomness.
At a low temperature the model plays safe. At a high temperature it takes more risks, which can make the writing more creative but also less accurate.
This is why asking the same question twice can produce two different answers.
Training has two main stages. In the first, called pre-training, the model reads vast amounts of text and learns general patterns.
In the second, the model is refined using examples of good answers and feedback from human reviewers, who rate which responses are more helpful and honest.
This second stage is why a modern assistant behaves like a polite helper rather than simply continuing a sentence.
Now, an important limitation. Because the model is built to produce plausible text, it can generate statements that sound confident but are false. These are sometimes called hallucinations.
The model has no built-in way of checking facts against the world; it knows only patterns.
Systems connected to a search tool or a trusted database make fewer mistakes, but nothing removes the risk completely.
For this reason, anyone using a model for legal or academic work should verify every claim and every reference, especially names, dates and citations.
To sum up: a language model predicts text, one token at a time, using attention to consider the context, and a degree of randomness to avoid repetition.
It is a powerful tool for drafting and explaining, but it is not a source of truth.
In the seminar, bring one example of an answer from a model that you checked, and tell us what you found.

qs.q: What is the basic training goal of a language model?
o: To store facts in a database.
To predict the next piece of text.
To translate between languages.
qs.why: هدف التدريب كله هو التنبؤ بالجزء التالي من النص.

qs.q: Why do models sometimes make mistakes when counting letters?
o: They are trained only on short texts.
They work with tokens rather than individual letters.
They ignore rare words.
qs.why: النص يُقطّع إلى وحدات، فلا يرى النموذج الحروف مباشرة.

qs.q: What does attention allow the model to do?
o: Choose a random word.
Correct its own spelling.
Look back at earlier tokens to see which matter most.
qs.why: تتيح له مراجعة الرموز السابقة وتحديد الأهم للتنبؤ التالي.

qs.q: A setting that controls how random the output is is called ___.
qs.why: الإعداد المسمى درجة الحرارة يتحكم في العشوائية.

qs.q: A model always gives exactly the same answer when the same question is asked twice.
qs.why: بسبب العشوائية قد يعطي السؤال نفسه جوابين مختلفين.

qs.q: What is the purpose of the second stage of training?
o: To make the model behave like a helpful assistant using human feedback.
To add more text from the internet.
To remove all parameters.
qs.why: يُصقل النموذج بأمثلة جيدة وتقييم بشري فيتصرف كمساعد مهذب.

qs.q: Why can a model produce false statements that sound confident?
o: It knows only patterns and cannot check facts itself.
It always copies from one source.
It refuses to use a search tool.
qs.why: يُنتج نصا معقولا لا حقيقة مؤكدة، وليس له وسيلة داخلية لفحص الوقائع.

qs.q: Users should check names, dates and ___ especially.
qs.why: أوصى بالتحقق من كل ادعاء ومرجع، خصوصا الأسماء والتواريخ والاستشهادات.

lines.t: Good morning. Why do some economies grow steadily richer while others stagnate?
Economists have long believed that the answer is largely innovation, meaning new ideas turned into products and methods.
Today I want to explain the economic logic of innovation, and why it is more puzzling than it first appears.
Let me begin with a feature that makes ideas different from most goods. If I eat a sandwich, you cannot eat it.
But if I use an idea, you can use it too, and the idea is not used up. Economists call this non-rivalry.
The result is that ideas are enormously valuable to society, since one discovery can benefit millions of people.
Yet they are hard for the creator to profit from, because others can copy them.
This creates the central problem of innovation policy.
If copying is easy, firms may not invest in research, since a competitor could imitate the product without paying the cost of developing it.
The traditional solution is the patent, which gives an inventor the exclusive right to use an invention for a fixed period, usually around twenty years.
In exchange, the inventor must publish how it works. Patents therefore reward invention while still spreading knowledge.
But patents are a compromise, not a perfect answer. During the period of protection, the owner can charge higher prices, so fewer people can afford the product.
Patents can also be used defensively, to block competitors rather than to protect real inventions.
Some economists argue that in fast-moving industries, such as software, patents slow progress, because every new product may infringe someone's existing patent.
There is a second challenge, which is risk. Most research projects fail.
A pharmaceutical company may test thousands of compounds to find one useful medicine, which can take over ten years.
Private investors are often reluctant to fund such uncertain work, particularly in the early stages. That is one reason why governments pay for basic research in universities.
The internet, satellite navigation and many medicines were first developed with public funding, although private firms later turned them into commercial products.
Third, there is the question of who actually innovates. It is tempting to imagine that large firms do most of it, since they have the money.
Evidence suggests a more mixed picture. Large firms are good at improving existing products step by step.
Newcomers, by contrast, are more likely to introduce radical changes, since they have nothing to lose from destroying the old way of doing things.
One famous economist called this creative destruction: new businesses replace old ones, causing losses and gains at the same time.
Finally, innovation affects people unevenly. A new technology may create skilled jobs while eliminating routine ones.
Overall employment may recover, but the individuals who lose work are not always the ones who find the new jobs.
This is why policies for retraining are considered an essential partner of innovation policy.
To summarise, innovation is valuable because ideas can be shared, difficult to finance because of risk and copying, and uneven in its effects on people.
Good policy supports research, protects inventors fairly, and helps workers to adapt.
For next week, find one recent invention and decide whether a patent was important to its success.

qs.q: What does non-rivalry mean for ideas?
o: Using an idea does not prevent others from using it.
Ideas can only be owned by firms.
Ideas lose value when they are shared.
qs.why: استعمال فكرة لا يستنفدها، فيمكن للآخرين استعمالها أيضا.

qs.q: A patent usually protects an invention for about ___ years.
qs.why: ذكر أن مدة الحماية المعتادة نحو عشرين عاما.

qs.q: What can happen when patents are used defensively?
o: They reduce the price of products.
They block competitors rather than protect real inventions.
They force firms to share secrets.
qs.why: قد تُستعمل لمنع المنافسين لا لحماية اختراعات حقيقية.

qs.q: Some economists think patents may slow progress in industries such as software.
qs.why: قالوا إن كل منتج جديد قد ينتهك براءة قائمة فيتباطأ التقدم.

qs.q: Why do governments often fund basic research?
o: Firms refuse to hire scientists.
Private investors are reluctant to back very uncertain projects.
Universities cannot publish otherwise.
qs.why: المشاريع البحثية محفوفة بالمخاطر ولا يتحمس المستثمرون الخواص لتمويلها مبكرا.

qs.q: Developing a new medicine can take more than ___ years.
qs.why: ذكر أن تطوير دواء قد يستغرق أكثر من عشر سنوات.

qs.q: Which firms are more likely to introduce radical changes?
o: Large established firms.
Government laboratories.
Newcomers with little to lose.
qs.why: الشركات الجديدة ليس لديها ما تخسره من هدم الطريقة القديمة.

qs.q: What problem does the lecturer identify about job changes caused by innovation?
o: Workers who lose jobs are not always those who get new ones.
New technology never creates jobs.
Employment falls permanently.
qs.why: قد يتعافى التشغيل عموما لكن المتضررين ليسوا دائما من يجد الوظائف الجديدة.
